opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting questions right now, and honestly one we're still figuring out.

The way I think about it goes back to my work on poker and games. When we were building poker AIs, one of the biggest lessons was that having the model actually *think* before acting, doing search and planning at the moment of the decision, made an enormous difference. It was worth far more than just scaling up the pre-computed policy. You could get gains from a bit of extra thinking time that would have taken orders of magnitude more training to match. That was a real eye-opener for me, and it's a big part of why I've been so excited about reasoning models.

But that doesn't mean you always want the model to think for a long time. Not every question deserves ten minutes of reasoning. If someone asks "what's the capital of France," you don't want the model deliberating. The ideal is that the model is adaptive. It should recognize how hard a problem is and how much is at stake, and spend compute accordingly. Humans do this naturally. You don't agonize over what to have for lunch, but you might spend weeks on a big career decision.

Part of this is a model capability question: can the model judge for itself when it's done, or when it's stuck and should keep going? And part of it is a product question: what does the user actually want? Some people care most about latency. Others would happily wait an hour, or even days, if the answer were meaningfully better, especially for things like research, hard math, or complex coding tasks.

What gets me most excited is that right end of the curve. Today we think in terms of seconds or minutes, but there's no fundamental reason models couldn't think for hours or days on genuinely important problems. If the answer is valuable enough, like a new drug candidate or a proof of an open conjecture, the cost of inference is trivial by comparison. So in the long run I think it's less about choosing between fast and slow and more about giving the system the judgment to pick the right point on that spectrum for each problem.

r001.rationale: The response argues for adapting thinking time to problem difficulty, stakes, and user latency preferences, but does not identify rapid user iteration as a reason for flexible thinking time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because for most of the history of the field, we basically only had one dial, which was how much compute you put into training. You'd train a bigger model on more data, and then at inference time it would just respond instantly. Every query got the same amount of thinking, whether you were asking what the capital of France is or asking it to prove a theorem.

And when you step back, that's kind of a strange way to build an intelligent system. Humans don't work that way. If I ask you a trivia question you answer immediately. If I ask you to make a hard decision, you sit with it. The amount of time you spend is proportional to how hard and how important the problem is.

My own intuition for this came out of poker, actually. With the poker bots, we found that letting the system think for even twenty or thirty seconds on a hand gave you a performance boost that was equivalent to scaling the model up by something like a thousand times. That was a huge wake-up call for me. It meant there was this massive lever that nobody was really pulling in the language model world.

So how should the balance work? I think the honest answer is that the model itself should learn to decide. You don't want a human hardcoding "spend three seconds on this, spend three minutes on that." You want the model to recognize that a question is easy and just answer it, and recognize that another question is hard and that it's worth burning more compute to get it right. And ideally the user has some say too, because the right tradeoff depends on the stakes. If I'm asking for a restaurant recommendation, I don't want to wait five minutes. If I'm asking for help with a cancer diagnosis or a complex piece of code, I'd happily wait an hour.

The thing people sometimes miss is that the cost structure is really favorable here. Training compute is a one-time cost that gets amortized, but inference compute is paid per query, and for a lot of high-value problems, people will pay a lot more than they pay today. If a model can do what would take a team of experts a week, spending a thousand dollars of compute on it is a bargain.

So I don't think of it as quick versus slow. I think of it as having two axes, and we've now unlocked the second one. Fast answers for the easy stuff, deep thinking for the hard stuff, and over time the model gets better at knowing which is which.

r001.rationale: The response supports flexible thinking time based on task difficulty and stakes, but it does not identify rapid user iteration with AI models as a reason.

astra-6.text:
I think the amount of time a model spends thinking should depend on the problem. If you ask a simple factual question, you probably want an answer immediately. But if you’re asking it to prove a difficult theorem or find a subtle bug in a large codebase, you might be happy to wait several minutes, or even longer, if that substantially improves the answer.

The challenge is getting the model to make that tradeoff intelligently. Is another second of reasoning likely to help? What about another minute? And what does the user actually care about—speed, cost, or getting the best possible answer? Ideally, models would adapt to those preferences rather than spend roughly the same amount of computation on every question.

r001.rationale: The response argues for flexible thinking time based on problem difficulty and user preferences, but does not identify rapid iteration with AI models as a reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think models should adapt how much they think to the difficulty of the question and how much the user cares about the answer. If you ask a simple factual question, you probably want a response immediately. But if you’re asking for a mathematical proof or a solution to a difficult programming problem, you might happily wait a few minutes if that substantially improves the result.

The interesting challenge is getting the model to make that tradeoff itself. Can it recognize when more thinking is likely to help, and when it should just answer? You don’t want it spending ten minutes on every question, but you also don’t want it giving the first plausible answer to something that really requires careful reasoning. I think that ability to allocate computation intelligently is going to be increasingly important.

r001.rationale: The response supports flexible thinking time based on question difficulty and user preference, but does not identify rapid user iteration with AI models as a reason for that flexibility.
